strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly articulates fundamental limitations of fixed tokenization (k-mers, BPE, single nucleotides) for DNA sequences and why learnable tokenization is needed

Thoughtful bidirectional adaptation: Successfully adapts dynamic tokenization from autoregressive models to bidirectional MLM with careful design (mask protection, gated residuals, probability-gated smoothing) that prevents mask-dependent artifacts
Strong empirical results: Achieves state-of-the-art on 10/18 Nucleotide Transformer datasets (14.2% average gain on histone markers) with 7× fewer parameters than GENERATOR (172M vs 1.2B)

Comprehensive analysis of learned representations: Clear demonstration through token distribution visualizations (Figures 2-3) and multi-chromosome analysis (Figure 3) showing adaptive allocation to functional regions
Robustness improvements: Demonstrates improved stability under insertions/deletions (Table 4: Stage 1 similarity 0.8512 vs 0.7506 for BPE), though SNV robustness is comparable

Thorough experimental validation: Includes ablative studies comparing with DNA-targeted baselines (MxDNA, PatchDNA) and stratified analysis across genomic features (promoters, introns, exons, repeats)
Reproducibility support: Detailed architectural specifications (Table 5), dataset construction, complete hyperparameters, and pre-training configuration facilitate reproduction
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core chunking mechanism adapted from Hwang et al. (2025); main contributions are engineering choices for bidirectional MLM rather than fundamental algorithmic innovation

Unfair comparisons and overstated claims: DNACHUNKER trained only on HG38 while GENERATOR used multi-organism genomes; on Genomic Benchmarks, DNACHUNKER ranks 3rd (3.29) vs GENERATOR 2nd (2.89); abstract claim of 'consistent improvement over baselines' is not universally supported

Missing critical ablations on design choices: No ablations for (1) mask protection mechanism—why enforce vs learn?, (2) cosine similarity choice for boundaries, (3) 0.5 threshold for hard decisions, (4) two-stage architecture necessity, (5) sensitivity to target compression ratios α and loss weighting λ

Overclaimed biological interpretation: Claims of 'structured' and 'biologically-informed' segmentation are correlational with existing annotations, not causal; no evidence that randomizing annotations would eliminate this pattern; no evaluation on out-of-distribution tasks
Limited evaluation scope: Restricted to human genome pretraining and downstream human tasks; generalization to other organisms unknown; only 1,000 ClinVar variants tested for robustness
Modest mutation robustness gains: InDel robustness improvement modest (0.8512 vs 0.7506); SNV robustness nearly identical to BPE (0.9987 vs 0.9993), undermining claims of 'mutation resilience'
Missing computational efficiency analysis: No wall-clock time comparisons; hierarchical encoder-decoder pipeline may offset parameter efficiency; actual FLOP reduction unclear

Insufficient statistical rigor: Standard errors reported but no significance testing; some improvements within baseline error margins (e.g., H3: 0.817±0.011 vs 0.806±0.005); no multi-seed stability analysis
Lack of sensitivity analysis: No ablations or sensitivity plots for compression ratio α, loss weighting λ, cosine similarity threshold, or probability-gated smoothing design choices

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly identifies limitations of fixed tokenization schemes for DNA sequences, with compelling examples of sensitivity to shifts and indels
Strong empirical results with parameter efficiency: Achieves state-of-the-art on 10/18 Nucleotide Transformer benchmark tasks while using 7× fewer parameters than GENErator (172M vs. 1.2B)
Thoughtful architectural choices: Mask protection mechanism and bidirectional smoothing demonstrate understanding of MLM pretraining requirements
Thorough analysis of tokenization behavior: Figures 2-3 and Table 4 effectively visualize how chunks adapt across genomic regions (promoters, exons, repeats) and show robustness under indels
Comprehensive experimental details: Extensive hyperparameter specifications and supplementary information support reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core contribution is adaptation of H-Net (Hwang et al., 2025) to bidirectional DNA MLM; no experimental comparison with H-Net provided. Mask protection is engineering-focused rather than methodologically novel

Oversold biological claims without sufficient evidence: Paper claims model learns 'biologically meaningful' patterns, but Figures 2-3 show only correlations with sequence complexity metrics (phyloP, repeats). No evidence that boundaries respect biological boundaries (splice sites, TF sites) or that tokenization predicts regulatory properties beyond what sequence statistics would capture

Unfair experimental comparisons with uncontrolled confounds: (1) GENErator trained on multi-species genomes while DNAChunker uses only human HG38; (2) 7× parameter difference (172M vs. 1.2B) makes comparison difficult; (3) Main network comprises 147.5M/172M parameters, with routing contributing only ~1.6M—improvement attribution unclear

Critical ablations missing: No comparison of learnable vs. fixed tokenization using identical architecture. No ablations for mask protection impact, number of stages, compression ratio targets, or similarity metrics. These are essential to isolate tokenization's actual contribution

Incomplete mechanistic understanding: Paper shows tokenization adapts to genomic regions but provides no analysis of what features encoder learns, whether chunks detect known motifs, or mechanisms behind boundary decisions. Analysis limited to 3 genes

Statistical and experimental rigor issues: (1) No p-values or significance tests despite overlapping error bars in many tasks; (2) DNA-targeted baselines (Table 3) use only 3 random seeds vs. 10-fold CV elsewhere; (3) Missing H-Net comparison despite being highly relevant related work; (4) No code availability mentioned

Unexplained performance patterns: Splice-site tasks show competitive but not best performance despite paper emphasizing robustness to mutations; prior work (Qiao et al., 2024) suggests segmentation-based schemes underperform on splice sites, but this tension is inadequately addressed

Confounded performance gains: Parameter efficiency gains compared to 1.2B-parameter GENErator are non-obvious given parameter difference. Fair comparison requires models of similar size. Reduced training data (human only vs. multi-species) could also explain differences

strengths: Clear practical motivation: DNA tokenization lacks natural word boundaries, making learnable segmentation well-justified and addressing a real gap in prior work
Strong empirical results: State-of-the-art on Nucleotide Transformer (rank 1.67) with 7× fewer parameters than GENErator baseline, and competitive performance on Genomic Benchmark

Compelling biological interpretability: Figures 2-3 convincingly demonstrate learned segmentation aligns with genomic features (shorter chunks at promoters/exons, longer at repeats) without explicit biological supervision
Robust to mutations: InDel robustness substantially outperforms BPE baseline (0.85 vs 0.75), with clear cascade error mitigation—practically important for genomics
Thoughtful technical design: Mask protection mechanism, masked residual gating, and bidirectional smoothing address real MLM-specific challenges with principled solutions
Comprehensive evaluation: Multiple benchmark suites, 10-fold cross-validation, comparisons to DNA-specific baselines (MxDNA, PatchDNA), genome-wide validation across chromosomes
Parameter efficiency: Achieving competitive/superior performance with 7× fewer parameters than baselines improves accessibility for genomics research
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: Core dynamic chunking mechanism heavily builds on H-Net (Hwang et al., 2025); main contribution is engineering for bidirectional+DNA setting—somewhat incremental for ICML audience
Incomplete design justification: Hard threshold of 0.5 (Eq. 2) lacks sensitivity analysis; two-stage architecture necessity not validated; cosine similarity choice not compared against alternatives
Missing critical ablations: No quantification of mask protection benefit, bidirectional smoothing importance, or necessity of two-stage design over simpler alternatives

Fairness of comparisons: GENErator trained on diverse genomes vs. DNAChunker only on human HG38; 1.2B vs. 172M parameter regimes makes direct comparison less clean; parameter-matched experiments would strengthen claims
Limited scope and generalization: Pretraining only on human genome; unclear how well approach generalizes to other species, unlike baselines with multi-species coverage
Incomplete analysis of biological alignment: While compelling visually, causal mechanisms remain unclear—why does MLM alone induce these patterns? Is alignment emergent or due to inductive bias?

Splice-site underperformance under-explored: Prior work suggests fine-grained tokenization benefits splice-site prediction, yet DNAChunker (0.931) lags GENErator (0.979); trade-offs and failure modes not deeply analyzed
Reproducibility gaps: No code release mentioned; missing implementation details (exact attention pooling, λ values, α values); Ratio loss weight (λ) and sensitivity analysis absent
Statistical rigor: Standard errors reported but no significance tests; some improvements borderline within confidence intervals; paired significance testing would strengthen claims
Incomplete hyperparameter analysis: Compression targets (α^(s)) not specified in main text; ratio loss weight (λ) sensitivity unknown; ablation studies on these critical hyperparameters missing

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear demonstration of limitations in fixed DNA tokenization schemes (sensitivity to shifts/indels, motif fragmentation)

Technically sound architecture with thoughtful design choices: mask protection mechanism, bidirectional boundary inference, probability-gated smoothing, and masked residual gating all carefully justified for MLM setting

Exceptional biological validation demonstrating learned segmentation captures meaningful genomic structure: motif fragmentation analysis (1.22 vs 2.47 tokens for BPE), robust segmentation under SNVs/InDels/SVs, and chunk-size ordering by biological information density
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across five diverse benchmarks (regulatory, epigenomic, variant-effect, long-range tasks) with proper cross-validation and standard error reporting

Practical efficiency: achieves strong performance with 172M parameters using only human genome pretraining, outperforming much larger multispecies models; inference FLOPs lower than fixed tokenization at long contexts
Excellent reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, pretraining protocols, finetuning specifications in appendices; uses public datasets and benchmarks
Controlled ablations demonstrate all components contribute; interesting finding that advantages widen with data diversity (multispecies training)
Thoughtful discussion of ethical implications with concrete safeguard recommendations
weaknesses: Methodological contribution is somewhat incremental: core techniques (hierarchical segmentation, ratio loss) largely from Hwang et al. (2026); main novelty is adaptation to bidirectional MLM and DNA-specific optimizations rather than fundamentally new methodology

Parameter count comparisons not entirely fair: DNAChunker (172M) compared to GENERator (1.2B) and NT-multi (2.5B) trained on multispecies data while DNAChunker uses only human genome; stronger comparisons to similarly-sized baselines needed

Limited theoretical insight: paper demonstrates that learned segmentation captures biological structure but provides limited explanation of why this architecture learns biologically meaningful boundaries or what objective properties encourage this

Incomplete ablation coverage: most ablations use reduced setup (50M params, 2B token budget); compression ratio targets and loss weights appear untuned; no sensitivity analysis on architectural choices (why two-stage specifically)

Mask protection validation is indirect: ablation shows removing it hurts performance but lacks direct evidence the model learns mask-conditioned segmentation patterns; could analyze segmentation on same sequences with/without masks
Limited generalization analysis: single-species (human) pretraining only; Table 5 shows multispecies helps but no explicit cross-species evaluation; unclear if approach transfers to non-human genomes

Missing failure case analysis: paper emphasizes successes but doesn't discuss when/why DNAChunker underperforms (e.g., splice-site and Genomic Benchmarks results); limited exploration of performance variation across genomic contexts
No statistical significance testing reported; some improvements are modest and within error bands; high variance on some tasks (H3K4me3: 0.660±0.045) raises stability questions
Training computational cost not reported: while inference FLOPs analyzed, hierarchical encoding adds pretraining overhead—no comparison of training time vs. fixed-tokenization baselines
Limited learned representation analysis: no probing tasks, attention visualization, or segmentation case studies on specific genomic regions; representation learning mechanisms unexplored

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation across five diverse benchmarks (NT, Revised NT, Genomic Benchmarks, DNALongBench, BEND) spanning short and long-range genomic tasks
Well-motivated problem with clear demonstrations of fixed tokenization limitations (Figure 1b-c showing k-mer brittleness and BPE motif fragmentation)
Thorough analysis of learned representations showing chunks correlate with biological functional regions (Figures 4-5) and remain robust to mutations across variant types (Table 6)
Detailed ablation studies confirm each architectural component (mask protection, residual gating, ratio loss) contributes to performance (Table 5)
Parameter efficiency demonstrated—172M parameters achieve competitive/SOTA results with only GRCh38 pretraining, with documented computational efficiency gains (Figure 3)
Extensive reproducibility details including hyperparameters, pretraining setup, and per-benchmark finetuning protocols across appendices
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: applies existing learnable tokenization techniques (H-Net, Byte Latent Transformer, BPE) to DNA MLM setting rather than introducing new algorithmic or theoretical advances

Causality between learnable tokenization and performance improvements not convincingly isolated—architecture conflates learnable segmentation with BiMamba encoders, specialized decoder design, and residual gating, making it unclear which factors drive gains

Modest empirical improvements on key benchmarks: +0.044 MCC over GENERATOR on NT, +0.023 over PATCHDNA on Revised NT (Table 2), second-best rank on Genomic Benchmarks, suggesting incremental rather than transformative advances

Pretraining corpus disparity undermines fair comparison—uses only GRCh38 vs baselines' multi-species pretraining; Table 5 shows tokenization advantage is corpus-sensitive (gap widens from +0.015 to +0.073 on multi-species data), yet no multi-species comparison conducted

Biological alignment shown but not mechanistically connected to performance—Figure 4 demonstrates motif preservation (1.22 vs 2.47 chunks) but lacks evidence this directly causes downstream improvements; no probing, attention analysis, or representation studies

Design choices appear ad-hoc and inadequately justified: cosine similarity for boundaries (Eq. 1) vs alternatives unexplored, compression ratios (0.33/0.33) lack ablation or justification, mask protection mechanism (forcing singleton chunks around [MASK]) presented as necessity but alternatives not considered
Missing ablation isolating tokenization from architecture—no comparison of learned tokenization combined with standard Transformer backbone to disentangle benefits from BiMamba/decoder innovations

Limited comparison to related learnable DNA tokenizers—only brief Revised NT comparison with PATCHDNA and MXDNA; insufficient analysis of what distinguishes DNAChunker from H-Net and other dynamic tokenization methods

Robustness analysis has interpretability issues: Stage 1 better than BPE under InDels (Table 6) but unclear if this reflects fundamentally better tokenization or simply less aggressive compression; similarity metric (γ=0.5) choice unjustified
Circular reasoning risk in biological validation—model trained on human genome with repeat downweighting, then same data used to show chunks align with repeats; held-out analysis lacking
Evaluation protocol inconsistencies undermine meta-comparison: 10-fold cross-validation vs 3 random seeds across benchmarks; no statistical significance testing despite modest margins in some cases

Key technical details under-specified: ratio loss optimization with non-differentiable hard boundaries (Eq. 6) unclear how sensitive to this; stage-wise LR scaling (√(Bs/Bref)·√(Dref/Ds)) non-standard and unjustified

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear illustrations of DNA tokenization challenges (shift sensitivity, motif fragmentation) and practical importance for genomics
Comprehensive evaluation across five diverse benchmarks (NT, NT-Revised, Genomic Benchmarks, DNALongBench, BEND) spanning regulatory, epigenomic, variant-effect, and long-range tasks

Thoughtful technical design for masked LM setting: bidirectional Mamba layers for segmentation, mask protection mechanism to prevent pretraining artifacts, masked residual gating to enforce main-network compute, stage-wise learning rate scaling

Compelling biological alignment: learned chunk sizes correlate with genomic function—exons receive short chunks (~14–16 bp), promoters/introns longer (~20–28 bp), SINEs longest with evolutionary divergence ordering (~32>28>17 bp)

Superior robustness to mutations: tokenizer more stable than BPE across SNVs, InDels, and structural variants of varying lengths (Table 6), suggesting context-dependent segmentation is more resilient than frequency-driven merges
Strong parameter efficiency: achieves competitive performance with 172M parameters (~14% of GENERator's 1.2B), demonstrating practical value for resource-constrained genomics applications

Extensive reproducibility documentation: detailed hyperparameters (Table 7), pretraining protocol (Table 8), finetuning details for each benchmark (Sections C.1–C.5), and public genome data source enable reproduction
Clear presentation with effective visualizations of tokenization problems and architecture design; well-structured paper with logical flow
weaknesses: Incremental technical novelty: core learnable chunking via cosine similarity and ratio loss (Eq. 6) is adapted from Hwang et al. (2026); main contribution is application to bidirectional DNA models rather than fundamentally new methodology

Modest performance improvements: +0.044 MCC over GENERator on NT benchmark (0.772 vs. 0.728), but GENERator has 7× more parameters; on Genomic Benchmarks ranks 3.29 vs. 2.89 for GENERator; sometimes second/third-best across tasks
Missing critical comparison with H-Net (Hwang et al. 2026), the most directly comparable prior work on dynamic chunking. This is a significant gap in related work evaluation
Ablation study (Table 5) restricted to small-scale setup (50M-param backbone) rather than full 172M model. Full-scale ablations would strengthen claims about component necessity
Lack of theoretical justification: paper empirically shows learned segmentation aligns with biology but provides no mechanistic explanation for why MLM should discover functional boundaries

No statistical significance testing: only standard errors/confidence intervals reported; no p-values or hypothesis tests for method comparisons, making it difficult to assess whether improvements are statistically meaningful

Single-organism pretraining: model trained only on human genome while ablation (Table 5) shows benefits increase with multi-species data (multispecies: +0.073 MCC advantage over BPE vs. +0.015 for human only), raising questions about generalization
Training cost not analyzed: paper reports inference FLOPs but omits wall-clock training time and computational requirements compared to baselines on equivalent hardware
